{{Short description|Combinatorial identity}}
In [[mathematics]], in [[combinatorics]], the '''Li Shanlan identity''' (also called '''Li Shanlan's summation formula''') is a certain [[combinatorial]] [[Identity (mathematics)|identity]] attributed to the nineteenth century [[Chinese mathematics|Chinese mathematician]] [[Li Shanlan]].<ref name=history>{{cite book|last1=Jean-Claude Martzloff|title=A History of Chinese Mathematics|date=1997|publisher=Springer Verlag|location=Heidelberg Berlin|isbn=9783540337829|pages=342–343}}</ref> Since Li Shanlan is also known as Li Renshu (his [[courtesy name]]), this identity is also referred to as the '''Li Renshu identity'''.<ref name=MI/> This identity appears in the third chapter of ''Duoji bilei'' (垛积比类 / 垛積比類, meaning ''summing finite series''), a mathematical text authored by Li Shanlan and published in 1867 as part of his collected works. A [[Czech Republic|Czech]] mathematician Josef Kaucky published an [[elementary proof]] of the identity along with a history of the identity in 1964.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Josef Kaucky|title=Une nouvelle demonstration elementaire de la formula combinatoire de Li Jen Shu|journal=M.-Fuzik. Cas..|date=1965|volume=15|pages=206–214}}</ref> Kaucky attributed the identity to a certain Li Jen-Shu. From the account of the history of the identity, it has been ascertained that Li Jen-Shu is in fact Li Shanlan.<ref name=history/> Western scholars had been studying Chinese mathematics for its historical value; but the attribution of this identity to a nineteenth-century Chinese mathematician sparked a rethink on the mathematical value of the writings of Chinese mathematicians.<ref name=MI>{{cite journal|last1=Karen V. H. Parshall, Jean-Claude Martzloff|title=Li Shanlan (1811–1882) and Chinese Traditional Mathematics|journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer|date=September 1992|volume=14|issue=4|pages=32–37|doi=10.1007/bf03024470|s2cid=123468479}}</ref>

==The identity==
The Li Shanlan identity states that

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^p {p \choose k}^2 {{n+2p-k}\choose {2p}} = {{n+p} \choose p}^2</math>.

Li Shanlan did not present the identity in this way. He presented it in the traditional Chinese algorithmic and rhetorical way.<ref>{{cite book|first=Andrea|last=Bréard|authorlink= Andrea Bréard |chapter=China|editor1-last=Robin Wilson|editor1-first=John J. Watkins|title=Combinatorics: Ancient & Modern|date=2013|publisher=OUP|location=Oxford|isbn=9780191630637|pages=78–79|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T02tF7NctM0C&q=Li+Shanlan%27s+identity&pg=PA79}}</ref>

==Proofs of the identity==
Li Shanlan had not given a proof of the identity in ''Duoji bilei''. The first proof using differential equations and [[Legendre polynomials]], concepts foreign to Li, was published by [[Pál Turán]] in 1936, and the proof appeared in Chinese in [[Jack Yung Chang|Yung Chang]]'s paper published in 1939.<ref name=MI/> Since then at least fifteen  different proofs have been found.<ref name=MI/> The following is one of the simplest proofs.<ref>{{cite book|last1=John Riordan|title=Combinatorial Identities|date=1979|publisher=Robert E Krieger Publishing Company|location=New York|isbn=0882758292|pages=15–16}}</ref>

The proof begins by expressing <math>n \choose q</math> as [[Vandermonde's convolution]]:
:<math>{n \choose q } = \sum_{k=0}^q {{n-p} \choose k}{p \choose {q-k}} </math>
Pre-multiplying both sides by <math> n\choose p </math>,
:<math>{n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{k=0}^q {n \choose p} {{n-p} \choose k}{p \choose {q-k}}</math>.
Using the following relation
:<math> {n \choose p} {{n-p} \choose k} = {{p+k} \choose k}{n \choose {p+k}}</math>
the above relation can be transformed to
:<math> {n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{k=0}^q {p \choose {q-k}} {{p+k} \choose k}{n \choose {p+k}}</math>.
Next the relation
:<math>{p \choose {q-k}} {{p+k} \choose {k}} = {q \choose k}{{p+k}\choose {q}}</math>
is used to get
:<math> {n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{k=0}^q {q \choose k}{n \choose {p+k}}{ {p+k}\choose q}</math>.

Another application of Vandermonde's convolution yields
:<math>{ {p+k}\choose q} =  \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}{k \choose {q-j}}</math>
and hence
:<math>{n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{k=0}^q {q \choose k}{n \choose {p+k}} \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}{k \choose {q-j}}</math>
Since <math>p \choose j</math> is independent of ''k'', this can be put in the form
:<math> {n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}\sum_{k=0}^q {q \choose k}{n \choose {p+k}}{k \choose {q-j}}</math>

Next,  the result
:<math> {q \choose k}{k \choose {q-j}} = {q\choose j}{j \choose{q-k}}</math>
gives
:<math> {n \choose p}{n \choose q} = \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}\sum_{k=0}^q {q \choose j}{j \choose {q-k}}{n \choose {p+k}}</math>
::::<math> = \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}{q \choose j}\sum_{k=0}^q {j \choose {q-k}}{n \choose {p+k}}</math>
::::<math> = \sum_{j=0}^q {p \choose j}{q \choose j}{{n+j}\choose {p+q}}</math>

Setting ''p'' = ''q'' and replacing ''j'' by ''k'',

:<math>{n \choose p}^2 = \sum_{k=0}^p {p \choose k}^2{{n+k}\choose {2p}}</math>

Li's identity follows from this by replacing ''n'' by ''n'' + ''p'' and doing some rearrangement of terms in the resulting expression:
:<math>{{n+p} \choose p}^2 = \sum_{k=0}^p {p \choose k}^2{{n+2p-k}\choose {2p}}</math>

==On ''Duoji bilei''==
The term ''duoji'' denotes a certain traditional Chinese method of  computing sums of piles. Most of the mathematics that was developed in China since the sixteenth century is related to the ''duoji'' method. Li Shanlan was one of the greatest exponents of this method and ''Duoji bilei'' is an exposition of his work related to this method. ''Duoji bilei'' consists of four chapters: Chapter 1 deals with triangular piles, Chapter 2 with finite [[power series]], Chapter 3 with triangular self-multiplying piles and Chapter 4 with modified triangular piles.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tian Miao|title=The Westernization of Chinese mathematics: The case study of the ''Duoji'' method and its development|journal=East Asian Science, Technology, and Medicine|date=2003|volume=20|pages=45–72|doi=10.1163/26669323-02001004}}</ref>
